Healthcare utilization is a critical metric for understanding the burden of chronic gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary diseases on both patients and the healthcare system. In the context of the Danish healthcare system, utilization patterns reveal how frequently patients interact with medical services and the modality of those interactions (physical versus virtual). This topic is particularly relevant for managing chronic conditions such as [[IBD]] and [[Primær skleroserende kolangitis (PSC)]], where ongoing monitoring and frequent clinical assessments are necessary.

For pediatric and adult patients with IBD, healthcare utilization remains consistently high. Both newly diagnosed and prevalent children with IBD average 15 hospital contacts during the reporting period [^src1]. The majority of these pediatric interactions require in-person visits, with 64% of contacts for newly diagnosed children and 69% for prevalent children involving physical attendance [^src1]. Adult IBD patients show a slightly lower but still substantial frequency of care, averaging 11 contacts for both newly diagnosed and prevalent individuals [^src1]. Similar to the pediatric cohort, most adult encounters are conducted in person, accounting for 67% of contacts for newly diagnosed adults and 64% for prevalent adults [^src1].

Patients with PSC also demonstrate significant healthcare utilization, reflecting the complex nature of the disease. Newly diagnosed PSC patients have a high frequency of hospital contacts, with a mean of 17 contacts (ranging from 2 to 38) and a median of 16 contacts (interquartile range 9 to 22) [^src2]. The modality of care for these patients is predominantly physical, with 65% of contacts occurring in person and 35% conducted virtually [^src2]. Together, these utilization metrics highlight the substantial clinical footprint of IBD and PSC, emphasizing the need for resource allocation and the growing integration of virtual care in managing chronic hepatobiliary and gastrointestinal conditions.
